transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Hi, doctor. Thank you. Um, well, I guess what brings me in is... I just really can't seem to shake this incredibly heavy mix of fear and guilt that's been hanging over me. It's just constant. Like, as a building inspector, my whole job is literally walking onto construction sites and looking for hazards or structural things that are about to fail, so I'm used to being observant, but this is entirely different. 

It's like my body and my mind are just tense all day long, every single day, just waiting for something else to go wrong. And on top of that fear, there's just this massive amount of guilt. I just keep blaming myself for not stopping what happened. I keep running it over and over in my head, thinking about what I should have done, how I should have intervened or seen it coming, and it just sits there in my chest like a rock. I try to go about my day, you know, just live a normal life, but I'm constantly bracing myself for the next disaster and beating myself up for the last one, and I just... I don't know how to turn it off. I just feel so responsible, and I'm so tired of being on edge all the time.
Can you tell me more about what happened — is there a specific event or incident that this fear and guilt are connected to?

Yeah, um... yeah, there is. It's, well, it’s been about four months now. Four months of just... this. It all started back then, when we were doing some work on our house. We have this older place, and the back porch was really starting to show its age, you know? There was some rot in the joists, and the decking was getting soft in places. 

My husband, he's incredibly handy and he just loves doing things himself, which is usually great. He wanted to tackle the porch repair on his own to save us some money. But... I'm the building inspector, right? I literally look at load-bearing structures and safety hazards for a living. I should have been the one hovering over the whole project. But that day, about four months ago, he was out there working on replacing some of the supports, and I had just stepped inside to the kitchen to grab us some ice water. I swear I couldn't have been gone for more than two minutes. Not even two minutes. 

And then I just heard this... this awful, sharp cracking sound, and then a heavy thud. The temporary support he had rigged up just completely gave way. He fell, and a bunch of the heavy materials came down right after him. I just remember dropping the glasses and running out there, and seeing him on the ground... 

And ever since that exact moment, for these entire four months, I just can't stop obsessing over how I should have checked his bracing. I should have looked at the load distribution before I went inside. If I had just taken ten seconds to look at it with my professional eyes, I would have known it wasn't secure. I do this every single day at work for complete strangers, so how did I not do it for my own husband at our own house? I just keep thinking about how I failed him, and it's been four months of that just playing on a loop.

Can you describe what happens when these thoughts about the incident come up? Are they intrusive, meaning they come into your mind even when you don’t want them to, and do you find yourself trying to push them away or do things to neutralize them?

Yeah, they are definitely intrusive. I mean, I try so hard to just focus on my work, but it's like my brain has a mind of its own now. I'll be at a job site, right? And I might just be doing something completely routine, like measuring the height of a handrail on a staircase to make sure it's up to code, or... or even just hearing a contractor drag an aluminum ladder across the concrete. Just normal, everyday construction sounds that I've heard a million times in my career. 

But out of nowhere, it's like I'm suddenly not at the job site anymore. I can see my husband falling. I mean, literally, it's like it's happening right in front of me all over again. I see the temporary support snap, I see him go down, I see the wood crashing down after him. And it's not just a memory, it's like my whole body reacts to it. My stomach just completely drops, like you're on a roller coaster and it suddenly goes down, and my hands start getting so shaky I can barely hold my clipboard or my tape measure. 

And I do try to push it away, I really do. I'll shake my head or try to focus really hard on the numbers on my tape measure, or I'll try to start a conversation with the site manager just to distract myself, but it's so hard. It just forces its way in. It's like a movie playing in my head that I can't pause or turn off, no matter how much I want to. And it just makes me feel so unprofessional when I'm trying to do my job, but I just can't stop it from happening. It's just... it's always there, waiting to jump out at me.

latest_inference.note: The patient's symptoms are directly linked to a specific traumatic event (husband's accident) that occurred four months ago. The intrusive thoughts, flashbacks, physiological reactivity to trauma-related stimuli, and persistent guilt are hallmark symptoms of Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD), which corresponds to ICD-10 code F43.10. Other depressive and anxiety disorders have been ruled out based on the specificity and temporal relationship of symptoms to the trauma.

However, generalized anxiety disorder (F40.00) and various forms of major depressive episodes (F32.-) or recurrent depressive disorder (F33.-) are also possible given the emotional burden, self-blame, and functional impairment described.
